newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FEATURE - Head of Hungary's Ikarus relishes job.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Head of Hungary's Ikarus relishes job.

text.p: Gabor Szeles is not one to rest on his laurels. The saviour of electronics firm Videoton has surprised many by taking on what seems an even bigger challenge -- turning round Hungary's ailing busmaker Ikarus.
After reducing 500 million forints ($3 million) in Videoton losses to zero inside two years, he says he could do the same within six months for Ikarus, once seen as a lost cause.
"I would not be here if I didn't believe it can be done," Szeles told Reuters, catching his breath on the way to his next company meeting.
Szeles was nominated president of Ikarus Jarmugyarto Rt, which is 64 percent owned by Hungarian privatisation agency APV Rt and 31 percent by Russia's AO Avtotraktorexport, in September.
"Ikarus is a much easier case than Videoton was," he says. "It has not lost its technology or its products and has lost only part of its market," he said.
The muscular Szeles, 51, who has a university degree in electrical engineering, remains president at Videoton, which he has nurtured to health in five years at the helm.
The company expects profits of 800 million forints in 1996 on sales of 20 billion forints, compared to 400 to 500 million forint losses in 1992 on sales of some 7 billion forints.
In the same period, Videoton's work force has grown to 10,000 -- 13,000 including joint ventures -- from 4,200.
Despite his impressive record, outspoken Szeles chooses to concentrate on the challenges ahead.

In the 1980s, Ikarus delivered almost 10,000 buses a year to the former Soviet Union. Orders slumped when the USSR broke apart, forcing the busmaker to scour the world for alternative markets, selling small volumes to Egypt, Iran, Taiwan and other developing markets.
The busmaker plans to increase its total sales to 2,500 buses in 1996 from roughly 1,500 units in 1996, Szeles said.
"The main difference is that we now offer comprehensive financing packages to go with the buses," he said.
He expects Ikarus to make around one billion forints profit in 1997 on sales of 12 billion forints, compared with 2.5 billion forints of losses this year on sales of 15 billion forints.
Current production utilises only about a quarter of Ikarus's capacity, but a run-up to full steam requires serious reorganisation, Szeles said.
"The present 50-50 ratio of productive and non-productive personnel has to be changed in favour of more productive personnel," he said.
"I hope that in the next years we can increase our (utilised) capacity to some 4,000 to 5,000 buses," Szeles said.
His plan has some of the ingredients that proved successful at Videoton.
"Much the same as with Videoton, some parts of Ikarus should be sold to foreign strategic investors like Volvo or Mercedes," he said.
A tender to sell Ikarus failed in spring this year as Volvo, the only foreign vehicle builder to bid, said it was only interested in some parts of the company.
APV declined to disclose details of Szeles's nomination as head of Ikarus, but his plans suggest he might have received permission to break the company up after all if he sees fit.
"We will clean up and hive off some parts of Ikarus and offer them to foreign investors. This is how Videoton achieved partnerships with IBM, Matsushita, Emerson, Philips and Siemens."
He added that his plans aim at creating an industrial park outside Budapest, built around the present Ikarus premises.

While the domestic market only demands 200 to 300 buses a year, Ikarus also expects to sell 500 to 600 buses to Western countries next year, mainly in the United States, where the company owns a minority stake in a joint venture that builds buses in Alabama.
The company also has projects underway to revive its sales in Russia by building buses there.

"The assembly plant in Tushino this year made 500 buses, and the number will increase to 600 next year," Szeles said. "We have also recently signed a contract for 500 units to be built in St Petersburg next year."
Ikarus's debts at around 12 billion forints roughly equal its registered capital, but Szeles hopes the debts can be managed.
"With the present business plan, we hope for a one-year moratorium on our debts," he said. "We plan to change some of them to mid- and long-term loans and keep repayments servicing manageable."
After six years spent reviving Hungarian enterprises, Szeles still feels this is his future.
"Crisis management is what I enjoy most," Szeles told a gathering of businessmen. "I will keep doing it as long as my strength lasts." ($1=158.36 Forint)
